articleTitle: Tunable narrowband external-cavity diode laser with an embedded fiber grating reflector
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: With the continuing development of coherent and multiplexed fiber systems, there is a need for compact, narrowline and efficient external cavity diode lasers that are broadly tunable. To this end, we have developed a new narrowline tunable laser in which the external cavity is formed by a fiber which contains an embedded Bragg grating reflector. This grating is formed holographically in the fiber core by a noninvasive technique. Relative to similar approaches that use a grating formed photolithographically on a polished fiber, this approach provides a grating with high environmental robustness, ease of fabrication and ease of tunability. Initial devices have utilized a multi-mode laser and achieved linewidths of 200 kHz and tunability over 2nm.

articleTitle: Frequency doubling of diode laser radiation
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Nonlinear frequency conversion of GaAIAs diode laser radiation into the blue spectral region by SHG or mixing is a promising technique for an efficient, compact, and modulatable source of coherent blue light in such applications as optical recording, underwater communication, and visual displays. In direct doubling, KNbO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> nonlinear crystal which allows room temperature noncritical 90° phase matching at 860 nm is used. Its large nonlinear coefficient makes it attractive in applications where limited fundamental power is available despite the small acceptance angle and bandwidth.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup> Due to the limited output power power of narrow stripe laser diodes, resonant enhancement of the fundamental has been used to increase the SHG efficiency. With a 143 mW laser diode output, which resulted in 108 mW of fundamental power incident on a monolithic KNbO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> ring cavity, 38 mW of 429 nm radiation was generated,<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> for a 35 % conversion efficiency.

articleTitle: Basic Limitations To The Signal To Noise Ratio In Fiber Systems
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: The need for long-haul transmission of analog and digital data in an increasing number of applications is focusing attention on a number of fundamental noise mechanisms which limit the performance of even ideal systems. The talk will consider the basic physics as well as the system implications of a number of these cases including self heterodyning noise in optical amplifier systems and conversion of phase to intensity fluctuations in fibers.

articleTitle: Coherent operation of a monolithic two dimensional array of laser diodes in an external cavity
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: There has been interest recently in the development of schemes for the coherent combination of the outputs from arrays of diode lasers so as to produce a high brightness output in the far-field. There have been successful demonstrations of both on-chip and external cavity techniques for generating coherent output from laser diode arrays. However up until now the sources used for external cavity demonstrations have been restricted to linear arrays of laser diode emitters. Here we report the first demonstration of coherent combination of a monolithic two dimensional array of laser diodes in an external cavity. The source used for this experiment was a 2-element by 5-element section of an incoherent monolithic array of Fabry-Perot lasers, that had etched 45-degree micromirrors to direct the laser output normal to the wafer surface. The device was fabricated at TRW and provided by the US Air Force. The detailed structure of this device will be described at the meeting. The front facets of the lasers were antireflection coated (reflectivity of about 3%) and the back facets were coated with a gold film to increase their reflectivity. Due to thermal limitations the array could only be operated in pulsed mode, typical pulse widths were one microsecond at 0.1% duty cycle.

articleTitle: High power collimated superluminescent diode integrated with micro fresnel lens
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Recently, high power and low coherent light sources are desired in optical sensing, photo-printing, fiber gyroscope, and so on, in order to avoid the effects of optical interference in the systems. For such purposes, a superluminescent diode (SLD) is most suitable device, however, the beam divergence is much larger than laser diodes resluting in the difficulty of applications to practical uses. To overcome such a problem, we have developed a compact collimated SLD using micro Fresnel lens.

articleTitle: Phase Conjugation Of Diode Lasers And Amplifiers
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: We will discuss coherent optical power scaling of semiconductor diodes by the phase-conjugate master oscillator-power amplifier (PC MOPA) approach currently in development at Hughes. A schematic representation of a 4-pass PC MOPA is shown in Figure 1. The optical output from a low power master oscillator, characterized by high quality spatial and spectral properties, is coupled into an array of diode optical amplifiers. The amplified beams are directed onto a phase conjugate mirror, back through the amplifiers and finally out of the system. Beams are directed through the various legs of the optical system by polarization selection using polarizing beam splitters, wave plates and Faraday rotators.

articleTitle: Tunable line-narrowed semiconductor laser for laser radar applications
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: High performance distance and velocity measurement systems are required to meet the demands of various aerospace systems. These systems include aircraft guidance and control, threat/hazard detection and avoidance, and control of large space structures. High performance measurement systems also are required in the manufacturing, control, and health monitoring of system components. In this paper, the development of a tunable, line-narrowed semiconductor laser for use in high precision range measurement systems will be discussed.

articleTitle: Semiconductor Laser Radar Techniques For High-precision Position And Velocity Sensing
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Semiconductor diode lasers are attractive sources for many laser radar applications because of their small size and light weight. The extremely wide modulation bandwidths available with these devices (˜100 GHz for optical frequency modulation, or 2:10 GHz for intensity modulation) can be used to achieve high measurement precision and/or fast update rate. Possible applications, for example, include "fly-by-light" aircraft flight control and robot control. A typical flight control system might require on the order of 100 linear position sensors with resolutions of 50 μm or less, strokes up to 50 cm, and update rates of greater than 200 sec<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. Our experimental and analytical results indicate that many such sensors can be multiplexed and serviced by a single transceiver using only one semiconductor laser diode.

articleTitle: Absorption spectroscopy using internal second harmonic radiations from diode lasers
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Internal second-harmonic (SH) radiations of few picowatts from various diode lasers have been used for absorption spectroscopy. An IR laser spectrometer with frequency marker using visible iodine lines at the SH radiation has been constructed. The internal SHG in the double-heterostructure lasers were reported recently. If the available power of internal SH radiation at ft detector 18 reasonably strong and the spectral width is narrow enough for high resolution spectroscopy, the internal SH radiation from a laser diode is an excellent light source for spectroscopy because of its single mode tunability. In this paper we would like to report visible absorption spectroscopy by SH radiations from AlGaAs (750-800 nm) laser and InGaAsP (1300 nm) DFB laser and their application for the frequency calibration.

articleTitle: Optical interconnection applications of diode lasers
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Interest in the application of diode lasers to interconnections within digital systems is growing. The trend toward multiprocessor computers requires an ever increasing number, speed, interconnectivity, and density of interconnections. Optical interconnection offer low loss, low dispersion, high bandwidth, freedom from crosstalk within the optical channel, and reduced impedance matching and groundplane requirements. The feasibility of a diode-laser-based optical interconnection system has been demonstrated in a multiprocessor computer in which 1024 interconnections were multiplexed onto two 400-MHz fiber links.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>

articleTitle: High power, uniform, grating coupled surface emitting lasers
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: The output power level and efficiency of grating coupled surface emitting (GSE) laser devices has remained low relative to edge emitting laser diodes. In this paper we discuss the fabrication of GSE lasers with high power and high differential efficiency comparable to those of edge emitting lasers. A schematic diagram of our GSE structure (grown by metallorganic chemical vapor deposition - MCVD) is shown.

articleTitle: Two Dimensional Optical Phased Array System
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: An integrated two-dimensional array of coherent emitters has been constructed from AlGaAs GRaded INdex Separate Confinement Heterostructure - Single Quantum Well (GRIN-SCH-SQW) material. The linear active integrated optic array contains: a Y-branch network to divide input optical power from one to ten branches, individual phase modulators and separate traveling-wave amplifiers for each of ten channels. The two-dimensional array is formed from two linear arrays which simulate a two-dimensional stack of linear arrays through the used of a beam combiner. The combiner overlaps the two arrays to produce a simulated 2-D array with an emitter spacing of 1.0 mm x 1.0 mm.

articleTitle: Highly coherent injection-locked laser diode arrays
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Injection-locking of a laser diode bar by a master single mode diode laser may provide a high power, narrow bandwidth, coherent source of cw laser radiation. By laser diode bar we mean a set of equally spaced laser diode arrays sharing a common substrate. In this experiment we have injection-locked<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup> two physically separated laser diode arrays to the same single mode master laser. The modulus of the mutual coherence function for the two injection-locked beams was measured to determine how well they could be coherently combined. The measured value .96 ±.06 was extremely close to the ideal value of unity.

articleTitle: Very precise phase/frequency control of confocal fabry-perot cavity coupled semiconductor laser
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: It is argued that ultra-narrow linewidth semiconductor lasers are attractive for the applications to precise measurements and high resolution spectroscopy, and coherent communication systems. The confocal Fabry-Perot cavity coupled semiconductor laser (CFP-LD) shows a wide band frequency noise suppression characteristics with natTllh linewidth. The FM characteristics of the CFP-LD had been reported elsewhere. The authors had carried out the experiment on the heterodyne optical phase-locked loop (OPLL) using two AlGaAs CFP-LDs of 10 kHz linewidths, with the phase error of 8.1 degrees and the frequency tracking error between two 1 asers of 0. ,lmHz at the integration time of 70sec [ 4]. The l inewidth of Uw het.erod~·ne signal under phase locking with PLL noise bandwidth of about 1 MHz 1.,ras less than 30 Hz, which was limited by the resolution bandwidth of the spectrum analyzer used in the measurement.

articleTitle: Broad-spectrum light emitting diodes for fiber-optic sensor systems
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Light emitting diodes (LEOs) with a broad emission spectrum (e.g., 750 to 900 nm) are a desirable optical source for a wavelength-division-multiplexing (WDM) based fiber-optic sensor network system. The number of sensors or channels served by such a broadband light source depends on the resolution of the WDM and the spectral width of the LED. The conventional LEOs with a spectral width of 30 to 40 nm are insufficient for most of systems requiring more than 10 channels for a common WDM resolution of 5 nm. In this paper, we report novel quantum-well LED structures capable of a 100 nm spectral width and high coupling efficiency into a multimode fiber. We have studied the generation of broadband light using emission from multiple states in an active layer consisting of either a single quantum well or two asymmetric quantum wells. Similaf concepts have been used for superluminescence diodes (SLDs) and wavelength switching, respectively. Basically, we have used the gain saturation effect in a high loss quantum well cavity structure to squelch lasing and force the device to simultaneously obtain gain from either the higher energy states in the same well or the higher energy wells. The loss has been introduced by reducing the mode confinement factor and adding an unpumped section to the cavity. With these designs, we have achieved a spectral width of 90 to 110 nm which, to our knowledge, the largest reported for this wavelength range. The quantum-well LED structure used in this work is shown.

articleTitle: High power semiconductor diode laser amplifiers
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: We are investigating a master oscillator-power amplifier system using a single-pass semiconductor laser amplifier. The advantages of a travelling wave amplifier over high-power external cavity or injection-locked oscillators include simplicity, lack of chirp under pulsed conditions, resistance to parasitic oscillations in undesirable cavity modes, and broad wavelength agility. The broad area (500 μm wide x 1000 μm long) amplifiers are fabricated from OMVPE-grown GaAs/GaAIAs material with a graded-index, separate-confinement heterostructure, single-quantum- well (GRIN-SCH SQW) design. The amplifier chips are mounted on diamond-turned heat sinks that provide nonvignetted optical access to both facets. The devices are then antireflection (AR) coated on both facets to inhibit lasing under high current conditions. The threshold current for the lasers typically increased from 1.3 A to 10 A with double-ended AR coatings.

articleTitle: Coherent addition of laser arrays using binary optics
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Coherent beam superposition has been demonstrated using binary-phase grating couplers. The method of Amplitude-to-Phase conversion has been used to completely fill the laser array aperture with a uniform beam, concentrating the far-field energy into the centrallobe. Diffractive coupling using the Talbot Effect has been demonstrated and miniature Talbot cavities with direct lateral mode control have been made. The lateral modes of the miniature Talbot cavity are controlled by the cavity length and position of the reflective coating at the output coupling mirror. A figure shows the design of this Talbot cavity along with a measurement of its far-field output pattern. The output is nearly diffraction-limited. The most promising techniques involve miniaturized cavity designs which can be monolithically integrated. The Coupled Micro-Cavity with hybrid reflective / diffractive binary optical elements is a compact cavity which is designed on a single substrate. A figure shows how the nearest neighbor reflective coupling works in this cavity. The experimental far-field output from this device is also shown.

articleTitle: Integrated amplifier-modulators fabricated in Grinsch-SQW structures by impurity induced disordering with fluorine
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: A variety of proposed photonic applications require the integration of active and passive waveguides on the same chip. One approach for achieving this integration involves disordering the quantum well in selected regions of the GRINSCH-SQW wafer while leaving the optical waveguide intact. Thus, passive waveguide regions can be imbedded in an otherwise active device. In this paper, we report a device in which active amplifiers and reverse biased phase modulators are integrated into a fundamental mode optical waveguide. The processing of the test structures started with the patterning of the implant regions with photo-resist followed by implantation of fluorine, followed by annealing. Fundamental mode ridge waveguides were formed using reactive ion beam etching. The stripe pattern of the waveguides was perpendicular to the stripe pattern of the implants so that the waveguides ran alternately through disordered regions and non-disordered regions. In addition to the integrated modulator/amplifier test devices, we cleaved bars which contained only modulators and only amplifiers. The nominal lengths of the amplifiers and phase modulators were 2 mm and 1 mm respectively. All devices received an anti-reflection coating on both facets to reduce the facet reflectivity to less than 0.5 percent.

articleTitle: Gain switching modulation of a semiconductor laser optical amplifier
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Wideband optical switches and modulators are expected to become key components in future high-speed optical fiber communication systems. A device that could modulate the signal and at the same time provide optical gain would prove beneficial. The output signal could then be split to, feed many fibers without excessive power loss [1]. Such switching elements should exhibit sufficient gain in the on-state, and high loss in the off-state (isolation) to provide a large switching ratio [2]. Semiconductor laser amplifiers have recently shown many promising features [3]. A long cavity length amplifier is preferred for reasons of high gain and isolation, though it will degrade the optimum performance due to increased spontaneous emission [4]. We report on measurements using an InGaAsP laser amplifier as a switching element at 1.3 μm wavelength. The device is a CSBH (Channeled Substrate Buried Heterostructure) laser with a 630 μm long AR coated cavity [5]. The effective reflectivity is estimated to 5·10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup> from gain ripple measurements.

articleTitle: Frequency stabilization of diode users
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: Ultra-stable diode lasers have been required for various application systems. In this presentation, we review performances of our frequency-stabilized diode lasers and their application systems. For reliable and accurate linewidth reduction, an electrical feedback was employed, and the half linewidth of a 0.83 μ AIGaAs laser was reduced to 560 Hz [1], which was about -25 dB from that of the Schawlow-Townes' limit of the solitary laser device. Optical feedback from an external confocal Fabry-Perot cavity was also employed to realize a moderately narrow Iinewidth of 20 kHz [2]. A compact module of this system was developed by using techniques of micro-optics. Figure 1 shows a photograph of this module [3]. This optical feedback was also employed to reduce the linewidth of a visible 0.67 μ AIGalnP laser to less than 50 kHz [4]. Optical feedback was combined with the electrical feedback for further linewidth reduction, and thereby the linewidth of an AIGaAs laser as narrow as 1 Hz was realized [5]. To avoid the instability of the optically feedback laser induced by the phase change of the reflected light from the external reflector, a phase conjugate wave generated from the other diode laser was injected into the laser. This novel optical feedback realized a stable linewidth reduction independent on the separation between the two lasers, as is shown by Fig. 2 [6].

articleTitle: Hybrid optic rf spectrum analyzer using waveguide type Bragg cell coupled with focusing lens and glass waveguide
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: The acousto-optic spectrum analyzer (AOSA) using a waveguide type Bragg cell, which consists of a Ti indiffused waveguide and a surface acoustic wave(SAW) transducer fabricated on a LiN'bOJ substrate, is promising as a compact RF signal analyzer. The integrated optic spectrum analyzer(IOSA) has been investigated as an AOSA using a waveguide type Bragg cell. In the IOSA, a Ti indiffused waveguide,a SAW transducer and two waveguide lenses are integrated on a LiNb03 substrate. However,the dynamic range of the IOSA is limited to less than 25dB by the scattered light in the Ti indiffused waveguide and the waveguide lenses. Scattering loss of the Ti indiffused waveguide is about 3dB since the waveguide length and the propagation loss caused by scattering are about 6cm and O.SdB/cm,respectively. Scattering loss of the waveguide lenses is about SdB. We developed a hybrid optic spectrum analyzer (HOSA) with a dynamic range of more than 30dB. In the HOSA, the scattered light is suppressed by setting the focusing lens outside of waveguides, limiting the Ti indiffused waveguide to the area where the guided light is diffracted by the SAW and leading the diffracted light to a photodiode(PD) array through the glass waveguide.

articleTitle: Study of optical signal distribution networks for coherent semiconductor amplifier arrays
publicationTitle: LEOS Summer Topical on New Semiconductor Laser Devices and Applications
abstract: The demand for high power semiconductor laser sources has lead to active research in semiconductor laser and amplifier arrays. We have evaluated three design concepts for providing coherent optical power to a semiconductor amplifier array. The proposed amplifier array will employ amplification of a distributed single frequency master oscillator signal to achieve coherent output power over a large aperture. Conceptually, the amplification scheme is similar to that of the microwave traveling wave amplifiers. Previous experiments have shown that approximately 1 mW of coherent signal per channel is sufficient to saturate the individual amplifiers of the amplifier array. The networks provide splitting and amplification of the master oscillator signal to meet the power requirement. The authors show the layout of all three network designs on the same chip. The experiments indicate that the tree design is the most desirable approach for distributing coherent signal on 25 micron pitch. The average output power per channel is very close to the goal of 1 mW and the average fractional coherence exceeds ninety percent.
